results.title: Tunisia sees biggest protest in years over economic hardship, shrinking freedoms
results.description: Tunisia sees biggest protest in years over economic hardship, shrinking freedoms “The state cannot built by concentrating all powers in the hand of one person”, Slah Eddine Salmi, head of the UGTT, told the rally. Sunday 18/10/2026 TUNIS Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years in the capital on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule. The demonstration, led by the major UGTT labour union and civil society groups, comes as Tunisia grapples with an economic crisis, worsening public services, recurring water and power cuts, and shortages of medicines and essential goods. Saied seized broad powers in 2021 and 2022, dissolving parliament, dismissing dozens of judges and ruling by decree, moves that opponents described as a coup. Rights groups say he has intensified a crackdown on civil society, journalists and opposition figures. Saied rejects those allegations, saying he is not a dictator, and has accused his opponents of engineering economic crises to fuel social unrest. In a rare show of unity, opposition parties from across the political spectrum joined lawyers, doctors, journalists, unemployed people and civil society groups in marching along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a focal point of the 2011 protests that helped trigger the Arab Spring uprisings. The protest poses a significant challenge to Saied after years of divisions weakened the opposition’s ability to mobilise large crowds. “Silence will no longer be acceptable … the state cannot built by concentrating all powers in the hand of one person”, Slah Eddine Salmi, head of the UGTT, told the rally. Hundreds of police were deployed across the capital. Protesters chanted: “No fear, power belongs to the people!” and “The prisons are full, people are hungry!”. They also revived the iconic slogan of the 2011 uprising, which in Tunisia was notably peaceful: “The people want the fall of the regime!” They called for the release of Saied’s critics and demanded an end to what they described as attacks on trade union rights. Some carried banners expressing frustration over unemployment and pollution. “Enough is enough! The country is collapsing. We suffer from power and water cuts, and one crisis after another,” said Yassine Gharseli, a protester from Sfax, about 250 km south of Tunis. “I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom and I’m not about to give up, even if I become the last voice in the country.”

results.title: 1,9 مليار ريال صادرات.. 19 شركة تمور سعودية تشارك بـ «سيال باريس»
results.description: يشارك المركز الوطني للنخيل والتمور، يرافقه أكثر من 19 شركة تمور سعودية، في معرض «سيال باريس 2026» بفرنسا خلال الفترة من 17 إلى 21 أكتوبر؛ بهدف تعزيز الصادرات الوطنية وتوسيع انتشار المنتجات بالأسواق العالمية. ويسعى المركز عبر مشاركته في المعرض، الذي يضم أكثر من 7500 عارض من 135 دولة، إلى تمكين شركات التمور من الوصول لأسواق جديدة. ويهدف لتوسيع شبكة العلاقات التجارية مع المستوردين وممثلي قطاع التجزئة والصناعات الغذائية لرفع تنافسية المنتجات. وتأتي المشاركة بعد تتويج المملكة بالمركز الأول عالمياً في قيمة صادرات التمور للعام الرابع توالياً. وبلغت قيمة الصادرات 1,938 مليار ريال خلال عام 2025م، محققة نمواً بنسبة 14,3% مقارنة بعام 2024م، وفقاً لبيانات مركز التجارة العالمي. أنشطة تفاعلية وتشهد الأجنحة السعودية، التي تضم المجلس الدولي للتمور، استعراضاً لجودة التمور ومنتجاتها التحويلية. وتتخلل المشاركة أنشطة تفاعلية وفعاليات تذوق، تبرز الاستخدامات المبتكرة للتمور في الأطباق بما يلائم أذواق المستهلكين الدوليين. وأوضح المركز أن هذه الجهود تدعم منظومة التصدير وتطور سلسلة القيمة عبر التكامل بين المزارعين والمسوقين والمصدرين. وتسهم المشاركة في تحقيق مستهدفات رؤية السعودية 2023، وتعزيز مكانة المملكة كوجهة رائدة دعماً للاقتصاد الوطني.

results.title: Lebanon seeks Israeli withdrawal, international presence in the south
results.description: Lebanon seeks Israeli withdrawal, international presence in the south Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met visiting French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot on Saturday to discuss the future of the international security presence in the south. Sunday 18/10/2026 BEIRUT Lebanon will press for an end to Israeli military operations at a new round of US-mediated talks on Tuesday, as Beirut also seeks international security arrangements to prevent a vacuum in the country’s south if United Nations peacekeepers withdraw at the end of the year. A Lebanese military delegation will present Beirut’s demands at a trilateral meeting in Tampa, Florida, on October 20, the Lebanese presidency said in a post on X on Saturday. The talks come amid continued Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon and a deadlock over the terms of a deal intended to end hostilities between Israel and the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met visiting French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot on Saturday to discuss the future of the international security presence in the south, where Israeli forces and Hezbollah have repeatedly clashed. Aoun reiterated Lebanon’s desire to extend the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which is due to expire at the end of the year. He said Beirut would welcome alternative arrangements if an extension proved impossible. “If this proves impossible, Lebanon welcomes any arrangement that ensures an international presence in the south, prevents a vacuum, and avoids placing the Lebanese army in direct contact with the Israeli army,” Aoun said in a statement. Barrot was in Beirut for a two-day visit focused on mechanisms for maintaining an international presence after UNIFIL’s mandate expires. The discussions reflect Lebanese concerns that the departure of peacekeepers could leave the south more exposed to renewed confrontation and place additional pressure on the Lebanese Armed Forces. Dispute over disarmament stalls implementation Lebanon and Israel have held several rounds of direct talks in recent months aimed at ending hostilities since a new war erupted on March 2, when Hezbollah attacked Israel amid the wider regional conflict. Under a framework agreement reached through US-brokered talks and signed in Washington on June 26, Beirut committed to disarming Hezbollah and dismantling its military infrastructure, alongside deployments by the Lebanese Armed Forces. Further Israeli withdrawals from the buffer zone its troops hold in Lebanon are tied to verified progress on those measures. Implementation has stalled, however, with the two sides divided over the sequence and conditions for carrying out the agreement. Hezbollah has refused to disarm while Israeli forces remain on Lebanese territory, while Israel has continued striking southern Lebanon. Lebanese officials have argued that the attacks undermine Beirut’s efforts to disarm the group. Israel, in turn, has said the Lebanese army is not yet capable of fully assuming the security responsibilities envisaged under the deal. The dispute has complicated efforts to establish a lasting arrangement along the border, where the withdrawal of Israeli forces, Hezbollah’s weapons and the deployment of the Lebanese army remain central to the negotiations. Beirut seeks international presence after UNIFIL The future of UNIFIL has added urgency to Lebanon’s diplomatic efforts. The force has monitored the border area for decades and played a role in maintaining communications and supporting stability during repeated rounds of conflict between Israel and Hezbollah. Aoun’s meeting with Barrot comes as Lebanon seeks to secure continued international involvement in the south, whether through an extension of UNIFIL’s mandate or another arrangement acceptable to Beirut. The Lebanese president’s warning against a security vacuum also highlights concern that the Lebanese army could be left facing Israeli forces directly if peacekeepers withdraw without a replacement mechanism. The next round of talks on October 20 will give Lebanon an opportunity to press its demands for an end to Israeli operations, although the continuing disagreement over Hezbollah’s disarmament and Israeli troop withdrawals remains a major obstacle to implementing the June agreement.
